case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.limits: The Court was addressing a device that made complete copies for private, non-commercial time-shifting. A commercial service that ingests works to build a product it then sells is a different fact pattern, and plaintiffs press that distinction hard.
case.holding: Selling a technology that can be used to infringe is not itself contributory infringement when the technology is capable of substantial non-infringing uses. Home recording of broadcast television for later viewing was held to be fair use.
case.case_name: Sony Corp. of America v. Universal City Studios, Inc.

quoted_in.lawsuit: Sony Music Entertainment v. Uncharted Labs, Inc.

claims.ip: Contributory infringement, defeated by the staple article of commerce principle imported from patent law: a device with substantial non-infringing uses does not make its seller liable. The fair use holding on time-shifting was necessary to establish that a substantial non-infringing use existed. The fourth factor turned on the absence of proven harm, with the Court declining to presume damage from unauthorised copying.
claims.tort: None. Sony is a copyright case and carries no product liability holding, which matters because it is occasionally cited loosely for the proposition that toolmakers are not answerable for downstream harm generally. It says no such thing.

policy.market_impact: The decision permitted an entire consumer electronics category to exist, and the home video market that followed became a larger revenue source for the studios than the theatrical business they were protecting. Defendants cite that outcome as the best evidence that predicted market destruction from a new technology is often wrong.
policy.regulatory_alignment: The Court expressly invited Congress to legislate if the balance was wrong, and Congress eventually did in adjacent areas through the Audio Home Recording Act and the DMCA. That sequence is the strongest historical argument that AI copyright questions belong to a statute rather than to case-by-case fair use, and it is quoted in almost every AI policy submission that argues for legislation.

evidence.black_box: None to speak of. The device was fully explicable and its behaviour reproducible by any juror who owned one, which is why the evidentiary fight was economic rather than technical.
evidence.technical_evidence: Survey evidence about how viewers actually used the machines, and testimony that some rightsholders did not object to time-shifting at all. The modern analogue is telemetry and usage data showing what a deployed model is actually used for, which is now discoverable and which most providers hold.

teaching.analogy: The Court borrowed the staple article of commerce from patent law: a seller of a component with lawful uses does not answer for unlawful ones. Test where it breaks. A videocassette recorder cannot be updated after sale, learns nothing, and its maker sees nothing. A hosted model is retrained, monitored, rate limited and shut off at will. Ask whether the doctrine survives when the seller retains continuous control over the article.
teaching.exercise: Take a current hosted model and rewrite its deployment so it looks as much like the Betamax as possible: what would have to be true about updates, monitoring, logging and post-sale control for the staple article of commerce defense to fit? Then state plainly what capability the provider would have to surrender, and whether any commercial provider would accept that trade.
socratic: Sony was decided on a device sold and forgotten. Does substantial non-infringing use mean anything for a service the developer can modify or terminate at any moment, and if not, what replaces it?

The Court refused to presume market harm from unauthorised copying. Twenty years later Grokster found liability on evidence of intent. State the rule that reconciles them, then apply it to a developer whose internal documents discuss the value of copyrighted training data.
Time-shifting was non-transformative and still fair. If a use need not be transformative to be fair, why has the entire training defense been built on transformation rather than on Sony?
The Court told Congress to act if it disagreed. Congress largely has not, for AI. Should courts read that silence as approval, as neglect, or as none of their business?

threshold.standing: Universal and Disney sued as copyright owners of broadcast programming. Uncontroversial then, and the modern contrast is sharp: AI plaintiff classes fracture over whether ownership of each individual work can be proven work by work.
threshold.legal_personhood: Not raised, and the silence is instructive. The recorder acted on a schedule its owner set, and no one suggested that timer-driven autonomy diluted the owner responsibility. That intuition is under real pressure from agentic systems that select their own actions.
threshold.liability_allocation: The plaintiffs skipped the direct infringers, who were their own viewers, and sued the manufacturer. The Court refused to let secondary liability substitute for an unwinnable primary case. Current plaintiffs make the same move against model developers rather than against the users who prompt infringing output, and Sony is the obstacle.

technology.outputs: A complete, unaltered copy of a broadcast programme, indistinguishable in content from the original. The fair use finding therefore rests entirely on purpose and market effect, not on any change to the work, which makes it the strongest available authority that non-transformative copying can still be fair.
technology.ai_mapping: The mapping is to the model-as-tool argument, not to training. Sony speaks to whether a developer answers for what users do with a capable system, so it governs misuse of a deployed model far better than it governs the ingestion that built one. Reading it as a training case is the most common misuse of it in current briefing.
technology.data_inputs: Free over-the-air broadcast television that the viewer was already licensed to watch at the moment of transmission. The copyrighted material entered the device from a source the user lawfully received, which is why the copying was time-shifting rather than acquisition.
technology.architecture: A sealed consumer appliance. Analogue capture from a broadcast tuner to magnetic tape, with a timer for unattended recording. Two properties decided the case: the manufacturer sold the device and then had no further contact with it, and the device made complete verbatim copies without transformation of any kind.
technology.human_agency: Total and located in the household. The viewer chose the programme, set the timer and retained the tape. Sony contributed the capability and nothing else, and the whole doctrine of substantial non-infringing use follows from that separation.

live_cases.name: Edelson, PC, et al. v. Anthropic, PBC
Neural AI, LLC v. Meta Platforms, Inc.
Neural AI, LLC v. X.AI Corp.

case.era_technology: Consumer analogue videocassette recorder with a tuner and a timer, sold outright to the public
case.why_ai_cites_it: It is the ancestor of every argument that a general-purpose tool should not be judged by its worst possible use. AI developers cite it for the principle that a model with real lawful uses is not unlawful merely because someone can prompt it into an infringing output.
